title: Charge, Current & Voltage
description: The basic quantities of every circuit — charge, current, voltage, power and energy — and how to keep their signs straight.

study.title: Charge and current
study.body: Electric charge $q$ is measured in coulombs (C); one electron carries $-1.602\times10^{-19}$ C. **Current** is the rate at which charge flows through a cross-section of a wire or element, in amperes: 1 A = 1 C/s. For a constant current $I$ flowing for a time $t$, the charge transferred is $Q = It$. Going the other way, charge is the integral of current: $q(t) = \int i\,dt$.

study.title: Reference directions
study.body: The arrow drawn next to a current is a **reference direction**, chosen before we know the answer. A positive value means positive charge really moves along the arrow; a negative value means it moves the other way. With double subscripts, $i_{ab}$ is the current from a to b through the element, so $i_{ba} = -i_{ab}$.

study.title: Voltage
study.body: Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge as charge moves between two points: 1 V = 1 J/C. Voltage is measured **across** an element (between two points), while current flows **through** it. The + and − marks are a reference polarity: $v_{ab}$ is the voltage of point a with respect to point b, and $v_{ba} = -v_{ab}$.

study.title: Power: the passive reference configuration
study.body: When the current reference arrow **enters the + terminal** of an element (the passive reference configuration), the power absorbed is $p = vi$. If the arrow enters the − terminal instead, the absorbed power is $p = -vi$. A positive result means the element **absorbs** power (a resistor, a battery being charged); a negative result means it **delivers** power.

study.title: Energy
study.body: Energy is power integrated over time, in joules (1 J = 1 W·s). For constant power, $W = Pt$. Electricity bills use kilowatt-hours: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 MJ. In every circuit the powers of all elements add up to zero at each instant: what the sources deliver, the other elements absorb.

study.title: SI prefixes
study.body:
Engineering values use prefixes that step by factors of 1000:
- p = $10^{-12}$, n = $10^{-9}$, µ = $10^{-6}$, m = $10^{-3}$
- k = $10^{3}$, M = $10^{6}$, G = $10^{9}$
Convert to base units before calculating, and watch the case: m (milli) is not M (mega). Example: 2.5 mA for 4 s gives 0.0025 A × 4 s = 0.01 C = 10 mC.

steps.title: Welcome to circuit theory!
steps.body:
An electrical circuit is a set of elements — sources, resistors, lamps, motors — connected in closed paths by wires. To describe what happens we use two main quantities:
- **current**: how much charge flows **through** an element
- **voltage**: how much energy each charge gains or loses **across** an element
A useful picture: current is like the flow rate of water in a pipe, voltage like the pressure difference that pushes it.

steps.prompt: Which description is correct?
options: Current flows **through** an element; voltage is measured **across** it
Voltage flows through an element; current is measured across it
Both are measured across an element
steps.explanation: Current is a flow of charge, so it passes **through** an element (like water through a pipe). Voltage compares two points, so it is measured **across** an element (like the pressure difference between the two ends of the pipe).

steps.title: Charge and current
steps.body: Charge is measured in **coulombs** (C). Current is the rate of charge flow, in **amperes** (A): one ampere means one coulomb passes each second. If a constant current $I$ flows for $t$ seconds, the charge that passes is $Q = I\,t$.

steps.prompt: A constant current of {{I|A}} flows through a lamp for {{t}} s. How much charge passes through the lamp?
steps.explanation:
For a constant current, charge = current × time:
$Q = I\,t$ = {{I|A}} × {{t}} s = {{I*t|C}}.
(1 A = 1 C/s, so amperes × seconds gives coulombs.)

steps.title: Reference directions
steps.body: Before solving a circuit we draw an **arrow** for each current. This arrow is only a **reference direction** — a guess made before we know the answer. If the current turns out positive, charge really flows along the arrow. If it is negative, it flows the opposite way. A negative answer is perfectly fine!

steps.prompt: The current in this resistor is labelled $i$ = −{{I}} A, with the reference arrow pointing to the **right**. What is really happening?
options: No current flows, because a current cannot be negative
steps.explanation: The minus sign says the real flow is **opposite** to the reference arrow, so {{I}} A of (positive) charge flows to the left, from b to a. Writing '$i$ = −{{I}} A to the right' and '{{I}} A to the left' describe exactly the same current.

steps.title: Voltage and polarity
steps.body: Voltage is the energy each coulomb gains or loses between two points: 1 V = 1 J/C. We mark a **reference polarity** with + and −. The notation $v_{ab}$ means the voltage of point a **with respect to** point b, so swapping the order flips the sign.

steps.prompt: Between points a and b we measure $v_{ab}$ = {{V}} V. True or false: then $v_{ba}$ = {{V}} V as well.
steps.explanation: Swapping the subscripts swaps the reference polarity, which flips the sign: $v_{ba} = -v_{ab}$ = −{{V}} V. Point a is {{V}} V **higher** than point b, so b is {{V}} V **lower** than a.

steps.title: Power: absorbed or delivered?
steps.body:
The power of an element is $p = vi$ **if** the current arrow enters the **+** terminal. This is called the **passive reference configuration**.
- $p > 0$: the element **absorbs** energy (a lamp, a resistor, a battery being charged)
- $p < 0$: the element **delivers** energy (a battery powering a lamp)

steps.prompt: The current $i$ = {{I}} A enters the + terminal of element A, and $v$ = {{V}} V. How much power does element A absorb?
steps.explanation: The current arrow enters the + terminal, so this is the passive reference configuration and $p = vi$ = {{V}} V × {{I}} A = {{V*I|W}}. The result is positive, so element A **absorbs** power.

steps.prompt: A cable carries a constant current of {{I|A}} for {{tmin}} minutes. How much charge flows through it?
steps.explanation:
Convert to base units first: {{I|A}} = {{I}} A and {{tmin}} min = {{tmin*60}} s.
$Q = It$ = {{I}} A × {{tmin*60}} s = {{I*tmin*60|C}}.

steps.prompt: A charge of {{Q|C}} passes steadily through a resistor in {{t}} s. What is the current?
steps.explanation: $I = Q/t$ = {{Q|C}} / {{t}} s = {{Q/t|A}}. One coulomb per second is one ampere, so millicoulombs per second give milliamperes.

steps.prompt: The charge that has passed through an element is $q(t) = {{a}}t^2 + {{b}}t$ C, with $t$ in seconds. What is the current at $t$ = {{t0}} s?
steps.hint: Current is the derivative of charge.

steps.prompt: For element B, $v$ = {{V}} V and $i$ = {{I}} A with the references shown: the current arrow points **out of** the + terminal. Find the power **absorbed** by element B (a negative answer means it delivers power).
steps.explanation:
The current arrow leaves the + terminal (it enters the − terminal), which is **opposite** to the passive reference configuration. So the absorbed power is $p = -vi$ = −({{V}} V × {{I}} A) = {{-V*I|W}}.
Negative absorbed power means element B **delivers** {{V*I|W}} — it acts as a source.

steps.prompt: An element has $v$ = {{V}} V and $i$ = −{{I}} A, with $v$ and $i$ in the passive reference configuration. Which statement is true?
steps.explanation: Passive reference configuration, so $p = vi$ = {{V}} V × (−{{I}} A) = −{{V*I}} W. The absorbed power is negative, so the element **delivers** {{V*I|W}} to the rest of the circuit. (Power is $v \times i$, not $v / i$.)

steps.prompt: A {{P|W}} appliance runs for {{h}} hours. How much energy does it use? Give the answer in joules (you may type a prefix, e.g. 7.2M).
steps.explanation:
Constant power: $W = Pt$ = {{P}} W × ({{h}} × 3600 s) = {{P*h*3600|J}}.
In kilowatt-hours: {{P/1000}} kW × {{h}} h = {{P*h/1000}} kWh (1 kWh = 3.6 MJ).

steps.prompt: Match each prefix to its multiplier
steps.explanation: Prefixes step by factors of 1000. Lower-case m is milli ($10^{-3}$) and upper-case M is mega ($10^{6}$) — a factor $10^{9}$ apart, so the case matters!

steps.prompt: Match each quantity to its SI unit
steps.explanation: The units are linked: 1 A = 1 C/s, 1 V = 1 J/C and 1 W = 1 J/s = 1 V × 1 A.

steps.prompt: With the passive reference configuration, a **negative** value of $p = vi$ means the element is delivering power.
steps.explanation: In the passive reference configuration $p = vi$ is the power **absorbed**. Negative absorbed power means the element actually supplies energy to the rest of the circuit, like a battery powering a lamp.

steps.prompt: A current of {{I|A}} flows for {{t}} s. How many electrons pass through the wire? Each electron carries $1.602\times10^{-19}$ C (type e.g. 6.24e16).
steps.explanation:
Charge: $Q = It$ = {{I|A}} × {{t}} s = {{I*t|C}}.
Number of electrons: $N = Q / (1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C})$ = {{I*t/1.602e-19}}. Even a small current is a huge number of electrons per second!

steps.prompt: The current into an element rises linearly: $i(t) = {{k}}\,t$ A for $0 \le t \le$ {{T}} s (and is zero before $t = 0$). How much charge has entered by $t$ = {{T}} s?
steps.hint: Charge is the integral of current — the area under $i(t)$.
steps.explanation:
$q = \int_0^{T} {{k}}\,t\,dt = {{k}}\,\frac{T^2}{2}$.
With $T$ = {{T}} s: $q$ = {{k}} × {{T}}² / 2 = {{k*T^2/2|C}}. Graphically this is the area of the triangle under $i(t)$: ½ × base × height = ½ × {{T}} s × {{k*T}} A.

steps.prompt: An element has a constant voltage $v$ = {{V}} V and current $i(t) = {{I0}}\,e^{-t/{{tau}}}$ A for $t \ge 0$ ($t$ in s, passive reference configuration). How much energy does it absorb from $t = 0$ to $t \to \infty$?
steps.explanation:
Power: $p(t) = v\,i(t)$ = {{V*I0}} $e^{-t/{{tau}}}$ W.
Energy: $w = \int_0^{\infty} p\,dt$, and $\int_0^{\infty} e^{-t/\tau}dt = \tau$, so $w$ = {{V*I0}} W × {{tau}} s = {{V*I0*tau|J}}.

steps.prompt: A {{V}} V phone battery is rated {{C}} mAh. Assuming the voltage stays at {{V}} V while it discharges, how much energy does it store (in joules)?
steps.hint: mAh (milliampere-hours) is a unit of charge.

steps.prompt: In this circuit $V_s$ = {{Vs}} V, the current is $i$ = {{I|A}} and the voltage across $R_1$ is $v_1$ = {{V1}} V. Using conservation of power, how much power does $R_2$ absorb?
steps.explanation:
The current leaves the + terminal of the source, so the source **delivers** $P_s = V_s i$ = {{Vs}} V × {{I|A}} = {{Vs*I|W}}.
$R_1$ absorbs $P_1 = v_1 i$ = {{V1}} V × {{I|A}} = {{V1*I|W}} (current enters its + end).
Total absorbed = total delivered, so $P_2 = P_s - P_1$ = {{(Vs-V1)*I|W}}.

steps.prompt: The current $i$ flows clockwise and the + and − marks define each element's voltage. Tap every element whose $v$ and $i$ follow the **passive reference configuration**.
steps.hint: Follow the arrow around the loop. At each element, ask: does $i$ go in at the + or at the − mark?
steps.explanation:
Passive reference means the current reference **enters the + mark** of the element (then $p = vi$ is the absorbed power).
- $R_1$: $i$ flows left to right and enters at its + mark: passive.
- $R_2$: $i$ flows down and enters at its − mark: not passive.
- $R_3$: along the bottom $i$ flows right to left and enters at the + mark on the right: passive.
- $V_s$: $i$ leaves through the + terminal, i.e. it enters at −: not passive. That is normal for a source that delivers power.

steps.prompt: A rechargeable battery that is being charged **absorbs** power.
steps.explanation: While charging, the charger pushes current **into** the battery's + terminal. With the passive reference configuration, $v > 0$ and $i > 0$, so $p = vi > 0$: the battery absorbs energy and stores it chemically. When it later powers a device, current leaves its + terminal and it delivers power.
